bib.title: Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection", Sudhir Varma and Richard Simon (NCI Biometric Research Branch), BMC Bioinformatics 7:91, published 23 Feb 2006 (peer reviewed, open access).
COVERAGE: 33657 of 33657 chars read, all 8 pages including references. Equations and some symbols came out garbled (eqs 1-8, delta, gamma), so I did not use them. Tables and figure text are readable. No embedded instructions found.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: On pure-noise data, the CV error of a CV-tuned classifier is far too optimistic, while its true error is 50%.
  number: Mean CV estimate 37.8% (shrunken centroids) and 41.7% (SVM) vs true error 50.0%; bias -12.2% and -8.3%.
  setup: "Null" synthetic data, at least 1000 datasets, each 40 samples (20 per class) with 6000 N(0,1) features and no class difference. True error measured on 20000 independent samples. Shrunken centroids used 10-fold CV to tune delta over 0.01-1. SVM used LOOCV to tune C (2^-5 to 2^15) and gamma (2^-15 to 2^3) on a grid, after picking the top 3 features by t-statistic inside each fold.
  quote: "Even though the mean true error is 50% (i.e. equal to randomly choosing the classes), the CV error estimate on the training set averages 37.8% for the optimized Shrunken Centroid classifier and 41.7% for the optimized SVM classifier."
  where: p.6; Table 1, p.5

- claim: A sizeable share of null datasets look good (error below 30%) purely through tuning on the CV error.
  number: Below 30% on 18.5% of datasets (shrunken centroids); 38% for SVM in the abstract.
  setup: Same null simulation as above.
  quote: "the CV error estimate for the Shrunken Centroid with the optimal parameters was less than 30% on 18.5% of simulated training data-sets. For SVM with optimal parameters the estimated error rate was less than 30% on 38% of "null" data-sets."
  where: abstract, p.1
  note: Table 1 gives 22.2% for SVM in the "training error<30%" column, which contradicts the abstract's 38%. The paper does not explain this. Cite 18.5% for shrunken centroids and flag the SVM figure as inconsistent.

- claim: The bias is not only a mean shift. It is large in a meaningful fraction of runs.
  number: Bias above 20% in 22.2% (shrunken centroids) and 25.3% (SVM) of datasets.
  setup: Same null simulation, from Table 1.
  quote: "On more than one-fifth of the random training datasets, the bias is more than 20% for the classifiers."
  where: p.6; Table 1 on p.5

- claim: Nested CV removes most of the bias. It is slightly pessimistic because each inner model trains on 39 samples, not 40.
  number: Shrunken centroids on null data: nested estimate 54.2% vs true 50.0%. SVM on non-null data: nested estimate 35.3% vs true 32.0%.
  setup: Outer leave-one-out over 40 samples. The inner loop reruns the whole tuning wrapper on the remaining 39 samples (10-fold CV for shrunken centroids, LOOCV for SVM). Non-null data has 10 of 6000 genes with a mean difference of 1. The same 40-sample, 20000-test-sample setup as above.
  quote: "The mean nested CV error estimate is a slight overestimate of the true error (54.2% compared to 50.0%), since the classifier used in each nested CV iteration is based on 39 samples, while the classifier used on the test set is trained on 40 samples." and "We obtain a mean nested CV error estimate of 35.3% compared to the true error of 32.0%."
  where: p.6

- claim: The rule is that every training step, including tuning and feature selection, must be repeated inside each CV loop.
  number: none
  setup: General argument, backed by the simulations.
  quote: "Proper use of CV for estimating true error of a classifier developed using a well defined algorithm requires that all steps of the algorithm, including classifier parameter tuning, be repeated in each CV loop."
  where: abstract, p.1

- claim: The bias comes from the variance of the CV estimates across parameter values, so it applies to any resampling scheme. It grows with the number of candidates K.
  number: none (the formula is garbled in the extraction)
  setup: Toy argument. The parameter takes K discrete values with identical true error E, and the resampling estimate is median unbiased. The text says the chance that the minimum estimate falls below E rises with K.
  quote: "Since the bias is caused by the variability in the estimates of prediction error for different values of the tuning parameters it is a general phenomenon."
  where: p.7

- claim: Total bias is the inherent bias plus the parameter-selection bias. Selection bias is always negative (optimistic). Low-variance resampling lowers it but may carry more inherent bias.
  number: none
  setup: Conceptual discussion. It names .632 bootstrap and bootstrap CV as lower-variance methods.
  quote: "The parameter selection bias, on the other hand, is always negative." and "If the inherent bias is positive, the parameter selection bias will subtract from it and possibly bring the error estimate closer to the true error."
  where: p.7

- claim: Alternatives to nested CV are a large independent validation set, or leaving out samples not used in tuning. Nested CV works if the outer left-out portion is small.
  number: none
  setup: Closing paragraph.
  quote: "If the number of samples left out at each step of the outer loop is not too large, this gives an almost unbiased estimate of the true error."
  where: p.7

- claim: Tuning on the test set is a separate error. The shrunken-centroid authors picked delta using the test error as well.
  number: none
  setup: Critique of Tibshirani et al.
  quote: "Thus the test set is used in the selection of the classifier parameters, which is problematic."
  where: p.4

- claim: Two older leakage mistakes are named. One is selecting features on all the data before CV (Simon 2003, Ambroise and McLachlan 2002, Reunanen 2003). The other is tuning parameters outside the CV loop.
  number: none
  quote: "One way is to use all of the training data to choose the genes that discriminate between the two classes and only change the classifier parameters inside the CV loop."
  where: p.2

LIMITS
- Synthetic Gaussian data only: n=40, p=6000, which is the microarray regime. The setup is not like typical tabular ML with n much larger than p.
- Only two classifiers were tested. The SVM was simplified: t-statistic top-3 feature selection instead of RFE, a fixed Gaussian kernel, and a grid search instead of a genetic algorithm. The authors say this "may potentially reduce the amount of bias obtained".
- Nested CV on shrunken centroids was only shown on null data. Nested CV on the SVM was only shown on non-null data. The abstract claims both were tested on both, but the results text does not show that.
- Nested CV is only slightly pessimistic (+4.2 and +3.3 points). The paper gives no cost analysis. Nested CV costs roughly the inner-loop count times more.
- The paper does not give the number of parameter values, a bias-vs-grid-size curve, or any comparison with repeated CV or bootstrap beyond a mention.
- The Table 1 and abstract mismatch (38% vs 22.2%) is unexplained.
- The paper's own LOOCV outer-loop description conflicts with the "10-fold" label on the Fig 3 caption (it says "nested within a LOOCV loop"). The shrunken centroids inner loop was 10-fold.

BUILDS ON: Duda, Hart and Stork 2001 (CV definition); Simon et al. 2003, Ambroise and McLachlan 2002, Reunanen 2003 (feature-selection bias); Tibshirani et al. 2002 (shrunken centroids); Peng et al. 2003 (GA/RFE SVM); Vapnik 1998; Chang and Lin (LIBSVM); Izuka et al. 2003 (earlier nested-style use); Efron and Tibshirani 1997 (.632+); Fu, Carroll and Wang 2005; Molinaro, Simon and Pfeiffer 2005 (comparison of resampling methods).

CODE: none in the paper (the simulation was in MATLAB 6.5, with no code given).

FIGURES (captions from the text extraction, not the figure tool)
- Fig 1, p.4: histogram of 10-fold CV error vs true error for optimized shrunken centroids. The CV estimates sit left of the true-error spike at 50%. This is the quickest picture of the bias.
- Fig 2, p.6: the same for the SVM with LOOCV.
- Fig 3, p.6: nested CV error vs true error for shrunken centroids on null data. The distributions overlap.
- Fig 4, p.7: nested LOOCV error vs true error for the SVM on non-null data.

PROBLEMS: Equations and Greek symbols were garbled in the extraction. pypdf printed font warnings (fontTools missing) that did not affect the text. I did not check the target note beyond its first lines, so the comparison with existing note content is left to the caller. Nothing else is missing.
